about: Points to handle, shown in the admin (Inbox › To do › Points, admin.js renderPoints; docs/ARCHITECTURE.md "Points to handle"). Written by agents: questions for an IMR trainer, nomenclature points, discrepancies between sources, content questions for Pierre. Pierre's state per point (status, notes, the trainer's answers) is his curation, in curation.json points, never here. The list's order is the priority: the most important first. Wording: neutral questions, never that IMR is wrong (rule C1). Fields: id (stable, never reused), kind (a key of kinds), subj (coral or fish), at (date added, Manila), title (the list's line), q (the question in plain words, shown big), ctx (context lines, folded), ask (the answer field under each photo), photos ([{f: a photo id of data.json or cand.json, with src, a, o, t as fallback when it leaves the app} or {none: why a slot is empty}]), src (sources: [{t, u?}]).

points.title: Which corals does IMR label Astrea in ReefCloud?
points.q: Which ReefCloud label would you give each of these corals?
ctx: Which corals does IMR label "Astrea" in ReefCloud: only Astrea curta and A. annuligera (Astrea in WoRMS and iNaturalist), or also the former Phymastrea, now Favites colemani, F. valenciennesii and F. magnistellata in WoRMS and iNaturalist, and maybe Paramontastraea salebrosa?
Slide 62's "refer to Astrea / Phymastrea" suggests the second; only a trainer can say.

Photos: 1 Astrea curta from abroad (one of the app's Astrea photos); 2 Favites colemani from the Philippines (one of the app's 4 F. colemani photos, under Favites); 3 Plesiastrea peroni from Dauin (a look-alike, from the Coral Finder's extra genera); 4 Pierre's Favites colemani near Dauin (iNaturalist observation 406194912); 5 and 6 Astrea curta from abroad (two of the app's Astrea photos, from two other observations), which Pierre doubts are Astrea; 7 Favites valenciennesi near Dauin (one of the app's Favites photos, a candidate Pierre added), which Pierre asks whether it is Astrea.
Until the answer the app changes nothing: its 4 F. colemani photos stay under Favites.
Waiting on this answer (Q47): if IMR calls these corals Astrea, Pierre's F. colemani near Dauin can serve as an Astrea photo (rule S2: his species-level photos stay usable as photos).

points.title: IMR's white Anacropora colony: skeleton or live colony?
points.q: Is this a coral skeleton (out everywhere, rule P6) or a live colony?
ctx: IMR lecture photo (Lecture 6, slide 19), Anacropora, Colony view: white branches lit by a flash on a dark background. It stands on the reef among live encrusting organisms, so it reads as a live (pale or bleached) colony, not a loose skeleton; but it looks like one.

It is the lead Branching photo of Coral basics (growth forms step) and a game photo of Anacropora. An RA review (2026-11-01, item 7) saw a wrong-answer comparison where Anacropora appeared "as a white skeleton on black" next to a live Alveopora close-up: probably this photo.
IMR lecture photos are never excluded automatically (rule P1), so it is not on the skeleton list (judging/skeletons.json). If it should go: × Exclude on Anacropora's page; if it stays, Resolved.

points.title: Chromis agilis or Pycnochromis pacifica
points.q: Allen & Erdmann (2020) and iNaturalist treat the Pacific populations of Chromis agilis as a separate species, Pycnochromis pacifica. Which name should RAs use for this fish at Dauin?
ctx: IMR reference list: Chromis agilis (Reef chromis), PDF page 19; WoRMS: Pycnochromis agilis. The IMR name stays in the app (rules C1, S2).
Allen & Erdmann (2020) describe the Pacific form as Pycnochromis pacifica; iNaturalist follows them (P. pacifica, taxon 1313512, about 345 observations; P. agilis, taxon 1316764).
The sourced check of 2026-11-14 found no photo of it in play and no Research Grade observation of iNaturalist's P. agilis in the Indo-West Pacific area the app takes photos from.
Since 2026-11-14 (Pierre, Q354 b) its candidate photos come from iNaturalist's P. pacifica; the admin says so beside its photos. The name players see is unchanged.

points.title: Halichoeres marginatus or H. annularis
points.q: iNaturalist treats the Pacific populations of Halichoeres marginatus as a separate species, H. annularis; WoRMS keeps them as one species. Which name should RAs use for this wrasse at Dauin?
ctx: IMR reference list: Halichoeres marginatus (Dusky wrasse), PDF page 50. The IMR name stays in the app (rules C1, S2).
iNaturalist: H. marginatus (taxon 102056) and the Pacific H. annularis (taxon 1474879), with 23 Research Grade observations in the Philippines at the check. WoRMS: one species, H. marginatus.

Fishes of Australia (H. marginatus) cites Kuiter (2010), who treats the Pacific form as a separate species, H. annularis, and Barber & Bellwood (2005), who found an Indian Ocean clade and a Pacific Ocean clade.

The sourced check of 2026-11-14 found no photo of it in play. Since 2026-11-14 (Pierre, Q354 b) its candidate photos come from iNaturalist's H. annularis; the admin says so beside its photos. The name players see is unchanged.

points.title: Two lyretail anthias: Pseudanthias squamipinnis and P. cheirospilos
points.q: The app has both Pseudanthias squamipinnis (IMR reference list) and P. cheirospilos (seen near Dauin). WoRMS and iNaturalist now restrict P. squamipinnis to the Indian Ocean. Should the list keep both lyretail anthias?
ctx: IMR reference list: Pseudanthias squamipinnis (Scalefin anthias), PDF page 32. The IMR name stays in the app (rules C1, S2).
P. cheirospilos (Pacific lyretail anthias; WoRMS 1909723, iNaturalist 1579632) is a separate species in the app, from Research Grade observations near Dauin, with 37 photos in play at the check.

The sourced check of 2026-11-14 reads WoRMS and iNaturalist as restricting P. squamipinnis (iNaturalist 127530) to the Indian Ocean: 10 of its 12 photos in play are from the eastern Indian Ocean (Andaman Sea, northern Sumatra), which iNaturalist still files under that taxon.
Pierre (2026-11-14, Q354 a): P. squamipinnis stays as it is for now, pending this question.

points.title: Angelfishes: the spine on the gill cover or on the cheek?
points.q: IMR's cue for the angelfishes says "Spine on the gill cover (opercular spine)"; FishBase's family summary puts the strong spine at the angle of the preopercle (the cheek). Which wording should the sheet and the cue use?

points.title: Wrasses: no visible teeth, or teeth that jut forward?

ctx: IMR fish presentation (fish.json f:Wrasses cues): "Thick lips, no visible teeth"; its look-alike line for the parrotfishes: "Wrasse: thick lips, no visible teeth".

FishBase, family Labridae: "Most jaw teeth with gaps between them; teeth usually jutting outward". The family sheet leaves this out until Pierre decides (rule C1: IMR's cue unchanged; Codex review #695).

points.title: Other species in view: confusion possible or not? (27 photos)
points.q: In each photo, could another fish be taken for the main one at the level the game asks (its family, or its genus for a circle-1 species)? Answer "no risk" (the photo plays) or "confusable" (it stays out).
ctx: Q323 (2026-11-09): the old count "other species in view" (m) is split in two, no risk of confusion (o, in play) and confusion possible (k, out of play, rule P3). An agent sorted the 1,047 photos that carried m (judging/FISH.md "Other species: the split"); these 27 were doubtful.

Meanwhile every one stays out of play (conservative). Photos 1-14 are photos you had in play (the auto-sort's adds): on their family page (Photos › Families) they now sit under "Other species, out of play"; Keep in play puts one back in one tap.
Photos 15-20 are stopgap or reference photos and 21-27 candidates still waiting: answer here and an agent applies it (tools/fish_judge.json, judging/fish).
The agent leaned "no risk" on 7 of them (photos 6, 7, 15, 17, 18, 23, 25), "confusable" on the others.

points.title: Diploprion: Soapfishes, or WoRMS's Liopropomatidae
points.q: The app teaches Diploprion (D. bifasciatum, s178) among the Soapfishes (Grammistidae, Diploprioninae); WoRMS and iNaturalist now place the genus in Liopropomatidae. Should the app keep it among the Soapfishes?
ctx: Found by the fish section of tools/taxonomy.json (2026-11-15, WoRMS and iNaturalist). Nothing changed in the app (rules C1, C5).
WoRMS: Diploprion (AphiaID 204362), family Liopropomatidae; iNaturalist (taxon 87970) the same. The app's teaching family Soapfishes holds Grammistidae and the subfamily Diploprioninae.

points.title: Ferdauia in WoRMS: the genus unaccepted, its species accepted
points.q: WoRMS marks the genus Ferdauia as unaccepted (→ Carangoides) while it keeps Ferdauia ferdau and F. orthogrammus as accepted species under it. Keep the app's Ferdauia ferdau as it is until WoRMS settles it?
ctx: Found by the fish section of tools/taxonomy.json (2026-11-15). The app shows Ferdauia ferdau (circle 3, s466); nothing changed (rules C1, C5).

WoRMS: genus Ferdauia (AphiaID 296636) unaccepted, valid name Carangoides; Ferdauia ferdau (AphiaID 1802000) accepted, its parent that same genus record. iNaturalist: Ferdauia, an active genus (taxon 1359822).

points.title: Cladobranchia: WoRMS's suborder, five suborders in iNaturalist
points.q: The Learn page groups the non-dorid nudibranch families under Cladobranchia, as WoRMS does; iNaturalist splits the same 15 families into Aeolidina, Dendronotina, Arminina, Janolina and Tritonina, with no Cladobranchia. Keep WoRMS's Cladobranchia?
ctx: Read 2026-11-16 for the Learn page's taxonomic groups (tools/seaslug_groups.json; Pierre, 2026-11-16: the true nudibranchs apart from the other sea slugs, Doridina then Cladobranchia). WoRMS is followed; nothing else differs: the 9 Doridina families and the other orders (Sacoglossa, Cephalaspidea, Aplysiida, Pleurobranchida) are placed alike (rule C5).

iNaturalist: Aeolidina (Facelinidae, Myrrhinidae, Flabellinidae, Trinchesiidae, Samlidae, Eubranchidae, Aeolidiidae), Dendronotina (Tethydidae, Bornellidae, Dotidae, Dendronotidae, Scyllaeidae), Arminina (Arminidae), Janolina (Janolidae), Tritonina (Tritoniidae). WoRMS: all 15 in the suborder Cladobranchia, by superfamily below it.

points.title: "Spanish dancer": Hexabranchus sanguineus, H. lacer or the genus?
points.q: The sources give "Spanish dancer" to Hexabranchus sanguineus (iNaturalist, WoRMS, Wikipedia, SEASLUG.WORLD, nudibranch.com.au), to H. lacer (SEASLUG.WORLD's article on the nicknames: the one Japanese divers know, since the genus was split) and, as "Spanish Dancers", to the genus Hexabranchus (iNaturalist; DAN's Alert Diver: "hexabranchs, also known as Spanish dancers"). The app shows the name, as information, on each taxon a source gives it to. Keep it so, or show it on one of them only?
ctx: Found by tools/seaslug_names.py (2026-11-17; Pierre, 2026-11-17: the sea slugs' common names and nicknames as information wherever names are shown). Nothing settled (rule C5); the game's choices stay scientific names.

H. lacer's own English names in iNaturalist: Decumbent Spanish Dancer, Mottled Spanish Dancer, Torn Spanish Dancer; WoRMS: mottled Spanish dancer. The Philippine Spanish dancers are mostly H. lacer (study 2.3; the list note's sources note, 1.5: Tibiriçá et al. 2023 split the genus).

points.title: Seven "sp. N" of the 2018 guide now have names
points.q: Papers since 2020 name seven "sp. N" of the 2018 guide (Gosliner, Valdés & Behrens, 2nd edition): Thecacera sp. 8 is T. pikachu, Tenellia sp. 20 T. nakapila, Phyllidia sp. 10 P. ovata, Goniobranchus sp. 43 Chromodoris kalawakan, Chromodoris sp. 11 C. quagga, Chromodoris sp. 12 C. balat, Nembrotha sp. 5 N. lorosae. Five are already in the species list under their names; C. quagga and P. ovata are not confirmed in the Philippines (rule C8). Nothing to rename. Anything you want done with them, such as a line on their species sheets giving the guide's old label?
ctx: Found by the literature watch (tools/seaslug_lit.py; the scan's note §3.2). Nothing settled (rule C5); the game's units are genera (Pierre, 2026-11-16), so players meet no change.

How each link is known: Thecacera sp. 8 and Nembrotha sp. 5, SEASLUG.WORLD's species pages, whose references cite the 2018 guide; Tenellia sp. 20, 8 of the 9 iNaturalist observations whose description says "Tenellia sp. 20" are identified T. nakapila now; Phyllidia sp. 10 (sp. 9 in the 2015 edition), the paper's synonymy; the three Chromodoris, the paper's treatments ("sp. 11 — Gosliner et al. 2018: 139").

Distinct Research Grade observers in the Philippines: T. pikachu 31, T. nakapila 27, C. kalawakan 16, C. balat 3, N. lorosae 3 (all confirmed); C. quagga 2 (one short, see the point on new species); P. ovata none at species level (the paper's Philippine record is a Dauin photo on Nudi Pixel, which rule C8 does not count).

Also named before 2018: Doriprismatica balut (13 observers, in the list) was Glossodoris sp. 1 of the 2008 guide and Doriprismatica sp. 1 of 2015 (Matsuda & Gosliner 2018). None of the 31 labels with 4 or more observers, Goniobranchus sp. 5 included, has a published name yet.

points.title: One name, several species: eight of our sea slugs are species complexes
points.q: Papers show eight species of our list to be complexes of several species, the others not named yet: Pteraeolidia semperi, Coryphellina exoptata, Samla bicolor, Phyllidiella pustulosa, Thuridilla gracilis, Costasiella kuroshimae, Jorunna funebris and Plakobranchus ocellatus. WoRMS and iNaturalist keep each as one species, and so does the app. A photo of one is sure at the genus (today's units), less so at the species. Keep them as single species, or mark them as complexes on their species sheets and for the species level later?
ctx: Found by the literature watch (the scan's note §4 and §5.3). Nothing settled (rule C5); no name to add or change. Observers: distinct Research Grade observers in the Philippines (tools/seaslugs.json, 2026-11-15).

Pteraeolidia semperi (162 observers, circle 1): Meshik et al. 2026, two clades living together in Vietnam, "at least two species within a broader and highly diverse species complex", species delimitation giving "about six and 20 units"; the clades differ mainly in colour, which depends on light and symbionts; no Philippine specimen.

Coryphellina exoptata (92, circle 1): Ekimova et al. 2026, "the Coryphellina exoptata species complex, represented by two species". Samla bicolor (49): the same paper, specimens "split into five monophyletic groups".

Phyllidiella pustulosa (61): Papu et al. 2022 (its Plazi treatment), still a species complex to solve, the name kept for one clade; the lectotype is "completely white", so no photo cue for the true form.

Thuridilla gracilis (31): Martín-Hervás et al. 2021, a complex of 13 species, T. gracilis, T. splendens, T. bayeri, T. ratna "plus nine undescribed species" (abstract summaries only). T. bayeri (3) and T. ratna (4) are in our list too.

Costasiella kuroshimae (53, circle 1, the "leaf sheep"): Jensen et al. 2014, "numerous distinct species that currently await description" (a search summary only); C. fridae was described from the Maldives in 2023 (Cunha et al.). See also the "Leaf sheep" point.
Jorunna funebris (153, circle 1): Tibiriçá, Strömvoll & Cervera 2023, "retrieved as a species complex in all possible partitions" (a search summary only).

Plakobranchus ocellatus (30): Meyers-Muñoz et al. 2016, 10 candidate species, P. papua (39, in our list) named that year; a "Plakobranchus sp. 6" of the 2018 guide (Philippines) still unnamed (search summaries only).

points.title: Phyllidia ovata among the P. picta and P. coelestis photos?
points.q: Wägele et al. 2025 described Phyllidia ovata (the 2018 guide's Phyllidia sp. 10) and found photos of it "in files of P. picta Pruvot-Fol, 1957 and P. coelestis in both iNaturalist and NudiPixel", with a Philippine record from Dauin. Our list holds P. picta (96 observers) and P. coelestis (154), both in circle 1, not P. ovata, which has no Philippine observation at species level on iNaturalist (rule C8). Should the photo judging check the P. picta and P. coelestis photos against P. ovata's description, and leave out those that match?
ctx: Found by the literature watch (the scan's note §4.2). Nothing settled (rule C5).

The paper's diagnosis of P. ovata: a white mantle "rarely with a tinge of blue", a black area on the central notum, "Large white conical tubercles have yellow apices", yellow rhinophores, a black line on the foot sole. Its range: "a narrow band in the Western Pacific from Japan south to Taiwan, Indonesia, and the Philippines".
P. ovata cannot serve as a look-alike cue yet: a species not confirmed in the Philippines stays out of the cues (rule C6). Its companion P. fontjei is not recorded from the Philippines.

points.q: Chromodoris alcalai (Gosliner 2021) "had been confused" with C. dianae before its description; the two are "separated by molecular evidence, external morphology, colour pattern, and internal anatomy" (SEASLUG.WORLD, on the paper). Both are in our list (C. alcalai 66 observers, C. dianae 52). A C. dianae photo taken before 2021 may show C. alcalai. Should the photo judging check older C. dianae photos, or prefer recent ones?

points.title: Tenellia, Phestilla or Trinchesia?
points.q: iNaturalist names Tenellia viei and T. goniophaga, which WoRMS gives as Phestilla viei and P. goniophaga ("alternative representation", for a "controversed genus allocation"); Korshunova, Fletcher & Martynov 2025 move T. nakapila to "Trinchesia", while WoRMS keeps Tenellia nakapila. The app follows iNaturalist's genera, with WoRMS's name beside. The units are genera, so a species' genus decides which unit its photos teach. Keep iNaturalist's genera, or follow WoRMS (Phestilla) for the two?
ctx: Found by the literature watch (`rename`; the scan's note §4.11) and the mode study (docs/reviews/2026-11-15-nudibranch-mode-study.md: 450 of our 452 names are WoRMS's accepted name, these 2 differ). Nothing settled (rule C5).

In the game today: the Tenellia unit holds T. bughaw, T. nakapila and T. puti; the Phestilla unit P. melanobrachia and P. sibogae. T. viei (9 observers) and T. goniophaga (5) are in the species list, not in the game.
The Trinchesia recombination is from a Plazi treatment's summary of the 2025 paper (not read); WoRMS cites the paper as the status source of Phestilla sibogae, P. melanobrachia and P. lugubris.

points.title: Watch: the guide's 3rd edition renumbers the "sp. N"
points.q: A 3rd edition of Nudibranch & Sea Slug Identification – Indo-Pacific (Gosliner, Valdés & Behrens, New World Publications; ISBN 978-1-878348-73-9) is announced for November 2026. The guides renumber their "sp. N" from one edition to the next, and the labels our tools keep and the iNaturalist notes they read mostly cite the 2018 edition ("Stiliger sp. 1 in NSSI2"). When it is out: use it as a source (the 2018 edition is not used: dated and DRM-protected), and map the labels to its numbers, each label keeping its edition?
ctx: A watch, nothing to decide before the book is out. The ISBN and the November 2026 date come from the publisher's announcement Pierre shared on 2026-11-17 (a screenshot of its post; not committed); a web search that day found no listing of the ISBN, only a search engine's summary of the publisher's page listing a 3rd edition, "updated and reorganized", with 500 new species and taxonomic changes (the page answered 503 and was not read). The undescribed study (2026-11-17, §3.2) had found no 3rd edition; 4 iNaturalist observations already write "NSSI3".

How the books renumber: Doriprismatica balut was "Glossodoris sp. 1" (2008), then "Doriprismatica sp. 1" (2015); one Gymnodoris is sp. 51 in 2018 and sp. 12 in 2008. Our labels name their edition (tools/seaslug_lit_source.json, "(NSSI2)"), and the papers' synonymies cite edition and page ("Gosliner et al. 2018: 139"), so a new edition breaks none of them.
Pierre, 2026-11-17 (Q389): the guide's "sp. N" other than Goniobranchus sp. 5 wait for a published name; the literature watch brings them in as papers name them.

points.title: Coral Finder 2022: do its pages compare Merulina with Hydnophora, and Duncanopsammia with Turbinaria?
points.q: On the Coral Finder 2022 pages, is Merulina compared in words with Hydnophora (pages 11-12, 17, 51, 62, 75), and Duncanopsammia with Turbinaria (page 50, also 9 and 74)? If so, on which page and by which feature? And on which page is the comment that sets Herpolitha (elongate) apart from the dome-shaped mushroom corals such as Halomitra (page 65 or 66)?
ctx: The four starred genera Alveopora, Merulina, Halomitra and Duncanopsammia have no card in Learn's Look-alikes deck: their look-alike pair cites only a shared Coral Finder box, and the deck takes only pairs a source compares in words (rule C2).

Coral Finder 2022 on Pierre's Drive is scanned with no text layer, so an agent could not read it. The earlier printing on his Drive (2009, look-alike pages 1-29) compares Alveopora with Goniopora (12 against 24 tentacles) and, in a page comment, Herpolitha with the dome-shaped free-living corals; it does not compare Merulina with Hydnophora, and its Duncanopsammia is the branching D. axifuga (D. peltata was then Turbinaria peltata).
Pages given here are data.json's pages for each genus. The study: docs/reviews/2026-11-18-classic-lookalike-pairs.md section 6.2.

points.title: Parrotfish juveniles: "striped, alike across species"?
points.q: The Parrotfish entry's juvenile note says small juveniles are striped and alike across species. Bellwood & Choat (1989), which the note cites, write that their 24 species can all be told apart as juveniles but two pairs, and some juveniles are not striped. Should the note stay as it is?
ctx: tools/fish_source.json t08 juv (class B): "Small juveniles are striped, alike across species, and change pattern as they grow."
Bellwood & Choat 1989 (abstract): "All species can be identified to the species level with the exception of two pairs of closely related species."

Fishes of Australia: Cetoscarus ocellatus juveniles "are white with a broad orange band around the head, a black ocellus on the dorsal fin"; Scarus niger juveniles "are dark greenish black, covered in small white spots"; Scarus altipinnis "small juveniles have a striped to mottled body with a distinctive yellow head" (Reef Life Survey: S. prasiognathos has "very similar juveniles").

Found by the juvenile sourcing of 2026-11-19 (tools/fish_juveniles.json). Nothing changed (rule C5): the entry keeps class B in the game; as a label, its species are Off, except S. altipinnis, Finer rank from its own source.

points.title: Emperor juveniles: Monotaxis grandoculis barred, the adult silvery
points.q: The Emperor entry's juvenile note says juveniles are not very different from the adults. Fishes of Australia describes Monotaxis grandoculis juveniles with broad dark bars, a black bar through the eye and orange-red tail lobes, while FishBase gives the adult as silvery grey. Does the note hold for Monotaxis?
ctx: tools/fish_source.json t11 juv (class B, Pierre, 2026-11-04): "Not very different from adults but not specific at all: early juveniles share a few patterns of stripes and bands, told apart by close examination." It cites Fishes of Australia 2756, the Monotaxis grandoculis page.

Fishes of Australia 2756: "Juveniles have 3 broad dark brown to blackish bars or saddles on the body (rear two extending onto dorsal fin), a black bar through the eye and an orange to reddish band along the outer caudal-fin lobes." FishBase: "Color of adult silvery grey with narrow dark scale margins".
Found by the juvenile sourcing of 2026-11-19 (tools/fish_juveniles.json). Nothing changed (rule C5).

points.q: Fishes of Australia says a published image of an Iniistius dea juvenile (Kuiter's) is a juvenile I. pavo. Are the game's 13 juvenile photos of I. dea all I. dea?

points.title: Iniistius pavo juveniles: two or three dorsal eyespots?
points.q: FishBase gives Iniistius pavo juveniles two large eyespots in the dorsal fin; Fishes of Australia gives three. Which count holds for the juveniles at Dauin?
ctx: FishBase: "Juveniles with black anal fin and two large ocelli, thinly edged with white, in dorsal fin". Fishes of Australia 296: "Juveniles have elongate anterior dorsal-fin spines forming a 'flag" and three ocelli along the dorsal fin."
The species sheet's juvenile line says "eyespots", with no count. Found by the juvenile sourcing of 2026-11-19 (rule C5).

points.title: Halichoeres biocellatus juveniles: two or three dorsal eyespots?
points.q: Reef Life Survey tells Halichoeres biocellatus juveniles from H. marginatus and H. melanurus by three dorsal-fin eyespots; FishBase gives the juveniles a pair. Which count holds?
ctx: Reef Life Survey: "Juveniles distinguished from H. marginatus (Dusky Wrasse) and H. melanurus (Hoeven's Wrasse) by having 3 dorsal fin ocelli and a black spot on the tail base." FishBase: "Juveniles and sub adults have a pair of ocelli on the dorsal fin which disappears with growth".
The species sheet's juvenile line says "two or three, the sources differ". Found by the juvenile sourcing of 2026-11-19 (rule C5).

points.title: Hemigymnus melapterus juveniles: two descriptions
points.q: Fishes of Australia describes the juvenile as greenish-brown with a diagonal white bar behind the pectoral fin; Reef Life Survey gives females and juveniles the adult's two-tone body, juveniles with a yellow tail. Which describes the juveniles seen at Dauin?
ctx: Fishes of Australia 245: "Juveniles are greenish-brown with a diagonal white bar behind the pectoral fin, before developing the pale anterior and dark posterior bicolor pattern."

Reef Life Survey: "Females and juveniles with a two tone body, head and fore body silver, divided by an oblique white bar from a black rear body with light vertical streaks on scales, dark patch behind eye and juveniles with a yellow tail."
The species sheet shows the Fishes of Australia description. Found by the juvenile sourcing of 2026-11-19 (rule C5).

points.title: Ctenochaetus binotatus juveniles: easily recognised, or easily confused?
points.q: A regional dive survey group calls the juveniles easily recognised by the yellow tail and the blue ring around the eye; FishBase's morphology page says the species is likely to be confused with closely related species. Which holds for the juveniles?
ctx: Solitary Islands Underwater Research Group: "juveniles often seen in the Solitary Islands Marine Park, easily recognised by the yellow caudal fin and blue ring around the eye." FishBase, morphology: "Ease of Identification likely to be confused with closely related species."
As a label (no effect on the game) it is Bold, from the juvenile-specific statement. Found by the juvenile sourcing of 2026-11-19 (rule C5).
